text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London ended slightly higher after a choppy session dominated by nearby spread activity. By the close, May stood $6 higher at $1,575 per tonne after an intraday low of $1,545. News that Indonesian 1997 coffee exports could be lower did little to move the market as many believe there is good supply of robustas.

Arabica futures in New York recovered from sharp morning losses to end modestly higher, buoyed by trade buying and speculative short covering, traders said. May closed up 0.25 cents/lb at 179.40 cents/lb, but also well off its peak of 183.00. Second month July settled 0.30 cents/lb firmer, to 165.05 cents/lb, while the back months finished up 0.90 to 2.90 cents/lb. Technically, traders said May coffee could trade sideways in the near-term between 173.50 support and 183.00 resistance. After the close the CSCE reported a slight fall in US certified coffee stocks as of April 4. Total stocks were down 750 bags to 82,328 bags. There were no bags pending grading.

EL SALVADOR - El Salvador's 1996/97 coffee harvest will end at around 3.2 mn 46-kg bags, with exportable output estimated at 3.0 mn bags, the Salvadoran Coffee Council recently said. Executive director Ruben Pineda said the harvest would end around 190,000 quintals (46-kg bags) above predictions of producer groups and the Salvadoran Foundation for Coffee Investigations (Procafe). Pineda stressed the figures still needed to be verified and checked. Pineda said that up to March more than 2 mn quintals had been exported.

INDONESIA - Indonesia's 1997 coffee production is expected to be some 30 per cent short of an original forecast 480,000 tonnes due to bad weather, the chairman of the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters (AICE), Oesman Soedargo, said. Incessant rains in 1996 and strong winds in coffee growing areas in Sumatra have affected the fruiting process resulting in a decline in coffee production, he said in a report obtained by Reuters. The total exportable volume would amount to some 220,000 tonnes this year, compared to with about 300,000 tonnes in 1996. Soedargo said domestic consumption would total about 120,000 tonnes this year, while carry over stocks would total 20,000 tonnes.

He also expressed concern over the possibility that there might not be much coffee left for export in the first and second quarters of the 1997/98 (October/September) crop year because of the decline in production and ongoing exports. Indonesia is the world's third largest coffee producer after Brazil and Colombia.

BRAZIL - Coffee exports in January 1997 amounted to 1.426 mn bags compared to 746,035 bags in January 1996. This brought cumulative exports in April/January 1996/97 up to 14.295 mn bags compared to 12.088 mn bags in April/January 1995/96. Total exports in 1995/96 reached 13.655 mn bags. Major countries of destination for Brazilian green coffee were the USA (2.105 mn vs 1.665 mn bags), Germany (1.721 mn vs 686,600 bags), Italy (1.243 mn vs 1.207 mn bags) and Japan (1.057 mn vs 823,000 bags). The largest markets for Brazilian solubles in April/January 1996/97 were Russia (682,000 vs 964,800 bags) and USA (443,100 vs 324,300 bags).
